sentences.text: He took one thing out of it and put four things in, and that is the arrangement he has kept for eleven years.
The thing he took was a mitten.

It was blue and it was hand-knitted with a pattern round the cuff in a way that nobody in Iceland does by accident, and it had belonged to his grandmother, and it had gone off a windowsill in the November of 2019 about four months before she died.
Its pair was in a drawer in his mother's room.

It had been in that drawer for six years because you do not throw away one of a pair when the person who made both is gone, and Ari had watched his mother open that drawer perhaps a hundred times and not say anything.
He knew the pattern round the cuff before he had the whole mitten out from under the slab.
There is a way of turning the eight-pointed rose at the wrist that his grandmother did and that is slightly wrong, and every person in that family can identify it across a room.
He carried it down the ridge inside his coat and he did not tell anybody for two days, and then he put it on the kitchen table.
His mother picked it up and turned it over and said, "Where." He told her.
All of it — the eight weeks of watching, the directions, the slab, the ninety-four things, the sheepskin folded at the back.
She listened the whole way through and then she went and got the other one and put the two of them together on the table, and neither of them said anything for a while.
It is not a good story about a woman being given something back.
His mother did not cry and did not thank him particularly.
She turned the recovered one inside out, looked at the wrist, said that the tension had gone at the end and that his grandmother's hands had been bad by then, and put both of them in the drawer.
They are still in the drawer.
Nobody wears them.
Ari has thought about that and has concluded that a pair in a drawer is a different object from a single in a drawer, and that this was the whole of what he had brought home.
Then she said: "What did you leave?" He had not left anything.
It had not occurred to him.

He went up the next weekend with an old fleece cut into four pieces and put them under the slab, and he has done something similar three or four times a year ever since — offcuts, mostly, and the wool that comes off the fence in June that he now collects on purpose.
He does not know whether it makes any difference to anything.
He is aware that a fox does not have gratitude and does not keep accounts and would take the fleece whether he had ever found the cache or not.
Ari is twenty-three and works on the boats and comes home in the winter.
The gloves still go.
His mother still loses between four and nine a year and complains about it in exactly the same words, and Ari has never once suggested that she stop.
He has told her where they are.
She knows.

She has never been up there and has never asked to go, and once, when he offered to take her, she said that it was two kilometres and that she had a farm to run and that if a fox wanted her gloves it was welcome to them.
Ari thinks she means it and also thinks she would rather they were somewhere than nowhere.
